questions.q: Why does round-robin load balancing fit LLM inference poorly?
options: Round robin cannot be implemented in any load balancer
It assumes every request costs roughly the same work, but prompt length, output length, and KV cache size vary widely between requests
Round robin only works with a single backend server
GPUs cannot be load balanced at all
questions.explain: Round robin assumes uniform request cost. LLM requests vary a lot in prefill length, generation length, and memory footprint, so strict rotation creates unevenly loaded replicas.

questions.q: What does least-outstanding-requests (least connections) routing do?
options: Routes every request to the same replica for consistency
Routes each new request to whichever replica currently has the fewest in-flight requests
Routes requests alphabetically by hostname
Disables load balancing entirely
questions.explain: Least outstanding requests uses current in-flight load as the routing signal, which tracks actual load far better than a fixed rotation.

questions.q: Why is session or prefix affinity especially useful for multi-turn chat workloads?
options: It guarantees the lowest possible cost regardless of load
It routes the same conversation back to the same replica so a cached prompt prefix (KV cache) can be reused instead of recomputed
It prevents the model from ever generating long responses
It is required by every cloud provider's networking layer
questions.explain: Session affinity keeps a conversation on the replica that already holds its cached context, avoiding the cost of recomputing a shared prefix from scratch on a different replica.

questions.q: In the example Nginx upstream configuration, what does `max_fails=2 fail_timeout=10s` do?
options: Limits each server to exactly two total requests ever
Pulls a backend out of rotation for a cooldown period after it fails health checks twice
Forces the server to restart every 10 seconds
Encrypts traffic between the load balancer and backend
questions.explain: This is a health-aware failure threshold: after two failures, Nginx stops sending traffic to that backend for the fail_timeout period, keeping a struggling replica from dragging down the pool.

questions.q: What is a reasonable approach for a load-balanced pool with mixed GPU generations or memory sizes?
options: Split traffic exactly evenly regardless of each replica's capacity
Weight routing so more capable replicas receive a proportionally larger share of traffic
Only ever use the slowest GPU in the pool
Disable load balancing for heterogeneous pools
questions.explain: A capacity-aware load balancer can weight routing toward more capable nodes instead of splitting evenly, which would let weaker replicas fall behind under equal load.
